h1: Content that brings visitors to a drinks brand's website
title: Content That Brings Drinks Site Visitors | Craft Beer School
desc: What to publish on a drinks brand's website so that the right people find it: answer real questions, show real places and keep every page honest.
teaser: The pages that bring visitors answer a question better than anyone else. A short list shows which ones a drinks brand should write.
standfirst: Content is not a blog calendar. It is a set of pages that each answer a question a customer actually has. Here is how a drinks brand chooses and writes them.
sections:
Collect the questions your customers ask: in the taproom, by message, on the phone, in reviews. Write them down in their own words. These are your content ideas. They cost nothing. Add what your keyword research shows, using the method in keyword research for a brewery website.

A question such as how long a tour takes or which beer suits someone who dislikes bitterness is a page waiting to be written.
The page types that earn their place

• Product pages: one per beer, wine or spirit, with style, strength, tasting notes and where to buy.
  • Visit pages: hours, address, directions, what to expect, how to book.
  • Explainers: what a style is, how to taste, how to serve, how a process works.
  • Food and serve pages: pairings or cocktail recipes you have tried.
  • Story pages: who you are and how you make things.

Not every brand needs all five. Begin with product and visit pages, which lead directly to a sale or a visit.
Write like someone who makes the drink

Your advantage is first-hand knowledge. A brewer can explain why a pale lager is cold-conditioned for weeks. A distiller can explain why a spirit is cut where it is. A winemaker can describe what a dry season did to the grapes. Say it plainly and with the right detail.

Avoid filler such as a long preamble about the history of beer. Get to the answer in the first lines, then add depth. Use short paragraphs and headings that describe what follows, so a person scanning on a phone finds what they need.

Check every fact: strength, ingredients, opening hours, prices. Do not make health claims. Do not write copy that encourages drinking more or targets under-age readers. Follow your local advertising rules, which differ by country and, in India, by state. Add a responsible drinking note where rules require it.

Date your pages or update them. A page about a seasonal beer that finished last year frustrates the reader and damages trust.
Make each page easy to act on

Every page needs a next step: a booking button, a map, a where-to-buy link or a sign-up. Look at the page as a first-time visitor and ask what they should do next. See website calls to action for taproom bookings for how to place them.

Link between your own pages. A tasting-notes page should link to the beer's product page. A style explainer should link to the beers of that style.

A small brand is better with ten strong pages than fifty thin ones. Plan one new page or one real update a month. Publish only when you have something specific and true to say. Search engines and readers both favour a site that is current and useful.

Do not copy descriptions from distributors or other sites. Duplicate text gives readers and search engines nothing new. Write your own, even if it is short.
An example page, step by step

Take a core beer, say a pale lager. The page opens with one line: what it is, its strength and how it tastes. Then a short paragraph on how it is made, with one real detail, for example that it is cold conditioned for several weeks. Then serving suggestions and food that suits it, a note on where to buy it and a clear button to book a visit.

That is perhaps 250 to 400 words. It answers the questions a customer would ask and gives a search engine a clear topic. Repeat the pattern for each beer, changing the details so that no two pages read alike.

Add photographs of your own product and venue, with plain descriptions in the image text for people who use screen readers. Accessibility is part of good practice and helps everyone.

Four habits undo this work. Writing for the search engine and not the reader leads to stuffed phrases and empty paragraphs. Writing about yourself only, with no answer to a customer question, brings visits from nobody. Letting pages go stale makes the site feel abandoned. And copying competitors' text makes you the same as them. Keep each page specific, true and useful.

Every quarter, look in Search Console at which pages are shown and clicked. In your analytics, see which pages lead to enquiries or bookings. Improve the pages that get attention but little action. Retire pages nobody reads. For the bigger picture, read SEO for breweries.
faqs: No. A blog is one format. Product, visit and explainer pages often work better for a small brand.
Can I use AI to write my pages?
You can use tools to help with drafts, but the facts must come from you and be checked. Pages with no real knowledge behind them tend to be generic and unhelpful.
As often as you have something true and useful to say. A steady monthly rhythm is enough for most small brands.
